At the edge of the lot, a row of young trees leans toward the road. The grounds crew planted them last spring, after a truck damaged the old fence. Every week someone ties the trunks to their stakes again, and every week the wind loosens the knots. This morning I watched one worker take off a glove to untangle a length of cord. She worked slowly because the bark had begun to split where a previous knot had pulled too tight. By the time she finished, the bus had come and gone. She gathered the loose cord, put her glove back on, and went to the next tree. The work will be waiting after the next storm.

Staff who receive a damaged specimen must record the condition of the outer package before opening it. The record should include the time of receipt, the carrier's name, and the condition of the seal. A photograph may be taken if the damage could affect the contents. The package should then be moved to the inspection bench, where a second member of staff can witness the opening. These steps help the laboratory establish what arrived; they do not establish when the damage occurred.

If the container is intact, the receiving member may continue with the ordinary intake procedure. Any liquid on the outside of the container should be treated as a possible leak until the source is known. Staff must wear the protective equipment listed in the bench procedure and keep other specimens away from the work area. A container with a broken cap or an unreadable label must remain in the inspection area. It cannot be released for testing simply because the accompanying form is complete.

The supervisor reviews the intake record on the same working day. Where the label is legible but the form differs from it, the supervisor contacts the sender and records the answer. No one should guess which description is correct. The sender may provide a corrected form, or the specimen may have to be returned. The supervisor's decision, the reason for it, and the name of the person contacted belong in the record. If the sender cannot be reached, the specimen stays on hold.

At the end of the shift, the receiving member checks that each held specimen has a visible hold notice and a matching entry in the register. The next shift should be able to find the container without relying on a verbal handover. A supervisor may authorize a change in storage location when space is limited, but the new location must be recorded before the container moves. This requirement applies even if the move will last only until morning.

The laboratory keeps the original packaging until the inspection is complete. Staff may discard it afterward under the ordinary waste procedure unless an investigation requires it to be retained. Questions about an uncertain container go to the supervisor on duty. This procedure is intended to preserve the evidence available at receipt and to prevent an uncertain identification from becoming a test result.
